title: Earnings per share and the P/E
desc: EPS, the P/E, and what a high P/E says about buyers’ hopes

cards.added: Feedback for options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy
cards.title: Same price, different bet
cards.situation: Acme and Northwind both trade at $50 a share. Acme earns $5 a share each year. Northwind earns $1. Which one are buyers expecting more growth from?

options.text: Acme: it earns more per share
options.feedback: Acme earns more today, so buyers pay only 10 years of its profit. High hopes show up as a high price for each $1 of profit.

options.text: Northwind: they pay $50 for $1 of profit
options.feedback: Buyers pay 50 years of today’s profit for Northwind. They expect big growth.
Same price, very different profit. Paying $50 for $1 of profit only makes sense if buyers expect it to grow a lot.

cards.title: Two numbers, two divisions
cards.text: **[[eps|EPS]]**, earnings per share, is profit ÷ shares. The **[[pe-ratio|P/E]]** is price ÷ EPS: how many dollars buyers pay for $1 of yearly profit.

blocks.tip: P/E 10 means buyers pay $10 for each $1 the company earns in a year.

cards.added: Tap notes written for the Academy (what each P/E means)
cards.title: High P/E = high hopes
cards.text: A high P/E isn’t “expensive” by itself. It tells you how much growth buyers already expect.

visual.title: P/E · three companies
visual.label: P/E 12 for Steady Power, 20 for Acme, 50 for Northwind

groups.label: Steady Power
groups.note: Buyers pay $12 for each $1 of profit: they expect slow, steady growth.

groups.label: Acme
groups.note: $20 for each $1 of profit: buyers expect some growth.

groups.label: Northwind
groups.note: $50 for each $1 of profit: buyers hope for fast growth.

cards.foot: If Northwind’s growth slows, buyers may pay less for each $1 of profit. A high-P/E stock can fall hard on small disappointments.

cards.title: Compare like with like
cards.text: A P/E means little alone. Compare it with **similar companies** and with the company’s **own past**.

cards.title: Find the P/E
cards.q: Acme made $20M profit and has 10M shares. The share price is $40. What’s its P/E?

options.feedback: 2 is the EPS, $2 a share. The P/E divides the price by it.
First EPS: $2 a share. Then the price ÷ EPS: buyers pay $20 for each $1 of yearly profit.
That divides the wrong numbers. First EPS = profit ÷ shares, then P/E = price ÷ EPS.
That multiplies the price by the profit. First EPS = profit ÷ shares, then P/E = price ÷ EPS.

cards.title: A P/E of 80
cards.q: Beta’s P/E is 80. Similar firms sit near 20. What does that tell you?

options.feedback: A high P/E isn’t a verdict. It shows big expectations, which is also a risk if growth disappoints.

options.text: Buyers expect much faster profit growth
options.feedback: Buyers pay $80 for each $1 of profit, four times what similar firms get. That’s big hopes, and a risk if growth disappoints.
That would be a margin. The P/E is price ÷ EPS: dollars paid for $1 of yearly profit.
A P/E doesn’t forecast the price. It shows how much buyers pay for $1 of profit today.
